item.title: Weaviate Launches Agent Skills for Developers
item.description:
Weaviate Launches Agent Skills for Developers

Weaviate introduces Agent Skills to empower developers building AI applications.

🔍 Overview

  • Agent Skills to empower developers building AI applications with Weaviate.
  • Agent Skills to help developers build and use AI agents with Weaviate more effectively.
  • Each skill is a folder containing instructions, scripts, and resources that agents like Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and others can discover to work more accurately and efficiently.
  • The skill is automatically discovered by compatible agents.

🧩 How it works

  • Works with any agent that supports the Agent Skills format.
  • Utility functions for the agent to directly interact with a Weaviate database.
  • Blueprints for complete end-to-end AI applications with state-of-the art guidelines for agentic infrastructure.
  • Use weaviate-best-practices to write or review Weaviate application code, with guidance on schema design, batch imports, and search.

⚙️ Key details

  • Each skill is a folder containing instructions, scripts, and resources.
  • The scripts and cookbooks rely on widely adopted third-party packages.
  • Not responsible for security of third-party components; new vulnerabilities may arise.
  • Users should run own security scans before executing any code and review packages flagged for known issues.
  • It is recommended to create a free cluster in the weaviate console.

🚀 Availability

  • Python 3.11+ required.
  • A Weaviate Cloud instance is needed.

🛠️ Capabilities

  • Create Collections
  • Explore Collections (Aggregation, Metadata, Schema)
  • Query Collections (Keyword-, Vector-, Hybrid Search) (Support filters)
  • Import Data (supports multi-vector and PDF ingestion)
  • Multimodal PDF Ingestion
  • Data Explorer
  • Retrieval Augmented Generation (Basic, Advanced, Agentic)
  • Query Agent
  • Query Agent Chatbot
  • Build a chatbot using the Query Agent
  • Build a multimodal RAG app for my PDF documents
  • Build an agentic RAG app
  • Search my Weaviate documentation for information about HNSW indexing
  • List all my Weaviate collections
  • Find products similar to ‘wireless headphones’ in the Products collection

📚 Examples

  • Search my Weaviate documentation for information about HNSW indexing.
  • List all my Weaviate collections.
  • Find products similar to ‘wireless headphones’ in the Products collection.
  • Build a chatbot using the Query Agent.

#Weaviate #AIagents #DeveloperTools #RAG #AgentSkills

item.title: AWS Completes Second ISO/IEC 42001 Surveillance Audit for AI Services
item.description:
AWS Completes Second ISO/IEC 42001 Surveillance Audit for AI Services

AWS successfully completed its second surveillance audit for ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the standard for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems (AIMS). This audit resulted in no findings and marks the addition of a new service to the certification program.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Audit Timeline: In November 2024, AWS was the first major cloud service provider to announce the ISO/IEC 42001 accredited certification for AI services. The second surveillance audit was completed in November 2026.
  • Audit Result: The audit concluded with no findings.
  • New Coverage: AWS DevOps Agent has been added as a new service covered under the ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification program.

📄 Services Under ISO/IEC 42001

The following services are covered under the AWS ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification program:

Service Status
Amazon Bedrock Originally certified in November 2024
Amazon Q Business Originally certified in November 2024
Amazon Textract Originally certified in November 2024
Amazon Transcribe Originally certified in November 2024
AWS DevOps Agent Added during the second surveillance audit in November 2026

💡 Why It Matters

This completion demonstrates the continuous commitment by AWS to responsible AI practices. With this independent validation, customers gain assurance regarding the commitment to responsible AI, which enables them to build and operate AI applications responsibly using AWS services.

🚀 Accessing Certifications

  • A full list of AWS services certified under ISO and CSA STAR is available on the AWS ISO and CSA STAR Certified page.
  • Customers can also access these certifications through the AWS Management Console for AWS Artifact.

#AWS #ISO42001 #AICompliance #ResponsibleAI #Certification

Source: AWS completed its second ISO/IEC 42001:2023 surveillance audit | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Quick adds Meta ads AI connector for marketing workflows
item.description:
AWS Quick adds Meta ads AI connector for marketing workflows

AWS Quick has added a Meta ads AI connector, enabling marketers to create, manage, and analyze campaigns using natural language while staying connected to the Meta ad management network.

🔍 Overview

The connector addresses the friction of manual data handling in marketing teams. Previously, data such as campaign results, creative assets, and inventory lived in separate systems like Meta Ads Manager, shared storage, and data lakes. Analysts often had to export reports and manually update campaigns, leading to slow insights. With the new connector, marketing teams can use one place to go from campaign planning to execution, acting on business insights directly in their ads without tool switching.

🧩 How it works

The Meta ads AI connector gives AWS Quick access to ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server operations. Installation involves navigating to Customize > Connectors in AWS Quick, signing in with Facebook, and selecting which Pages, Businesses, and Instagram accounts AWS Quick can access. Once connected, users can interact with the system via natural language prompts. The system can combine Meta ad management data with first- and third-party data sources to generate dashboards, documents, slide decks, and automated workflows. It also integrates with fal.ai’s image, audio, and video models within the same workflow to test creative ideas.

⚙️ Key details

The connector supports specific capabilities for managing ad lifecycle tasks:

  • Plan and launch campaigns: Drafts campaign, ad set, and ad settings from an approved brief; flags missing budget and audience decisions; runs pre-launch checks for naming, UTM tags, budget, and special ad categories.
  • Analyze and share performance: Tracks spend, CTR, and ROAS at various levels; compares results to the media plan; builds weekly decks of top ads, weak ads, and next tests; allows leaders to review decks and ask follow-up questions.
  • Refresh creative and audiences: Flags creative fatigue when frequency rises and CTR falls.
  • Pulling insights and creation: Supports creating product catalogs and editing or creating new campaigns.

The system also executes specific prompt-based outputs, such as turning past campaign results into an eight-slide launch-plan deck or building a dashboard comparing spend, leads, and cost per lead for two ad sets.

💡 Why it matters

By automating the path from insight to action, the connector reduces manual handoffs and tool switching. Marketing teams can spend more time reaching customers and testing more creative ideas, as supported by the integration of fal.ai media models.

#AWS #MetaAds #MarketingAutomation #AI

Source: Meta ads is now available in AWS Quick | Amazon Web Services

item.title: N-able cyberattack disrupts Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services
item.description:
N-able cyberattack disrupts Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services

N-able reported a cyberattack that breached a server in its Hosted Cloud environment, leading to a worldwide outage of the Mail Assume and SpamExperts services.

🔍 Overview

  • Attackers breached one of N-able’s servers, causing a major outage of Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services worldwide.
  • The outage initially was attributed to a “combination of platform configuration and service dependencies.”
  • N-able later confirmed unauthorized access to a server in the Hosted Cloud environment.

📅 Timeline

  • On Tuesday, N-able described the disruption as a configuration and dependency issue affecting the Americas, Asia‑Pacific, and Europe.
  • The following day, UI and API access were disabled and unauthorized server access was confirmed.
  • An email alert was sent to customers after the attack was detected.

⚙️ Impact

  • Email flow and spam filtering continued to operate; N-able said there is no evidence that attackers accessed customer data or mailboxes.
  • Customers could not sign in to the control panel, view or release quarantined messages, review logs, or modify domain configurations until services are restored.
  • The management portal (dashboard) and supporting services for quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization were taken down.

🛡️ Response

  • N-able disabled UI and API access, took down the management portal, and began mitigation steps.
  • The company is hardening services to reduce the risk of recurrence.
  • Investigation is ongoing, with no current evidence of compromised customer data.
  • N-able clarified that the incident is unrelated to a separate N‑central outage caused by more than 30 zero‑day flaws.

💡 Why it matters

  • Highlights the risk of unauthorized server access even when core email delivery remains functional.
  • Demonstrates the importance of rapid customer communication and service isolation during a security incident.
  • Shows that a single breached server can impact globally distributed cloud email security services.

#N-able #Cyberattack #EmailSecurity #CloudOutage

Source: N-able says recent security breach led to major service outage

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 reaches GA and is available on Lakebase
item.description:
PostgreSQL 19 reaches GA and is available on Lakebase

PostgreSQL 19 reached general availability today and is already available on Lakebase. Several engineers on the Lakebase team are PostgreSQL committers and contributors who worked on this release directly, from query plan advice to shared memory, locale handling, and release management. New major versions often take weeks to reach other managed PostgreSQL services.

🔍 Overview

PostgreSQL 19 is a practical release with no single headline feature that changes what PostgreSQL is. Instead, version 19 goes after operational problems that database teams know well:

  • Bloated tables
  • Unstable query plans
  • Replica lag
  • Incomplete statistics
  • Maintenance work that is hard to run safely in production

🧩 Key Features

  • REPACK — reclaims space while normal reads and writes continue during most of the operation
  • pg_plan_advice — describes planner decisions as advice, applies supplied advice, and reports whether it was followed
  • pg_stash_advice — stores advice by query ID and applies it automatically when a matching query is planned

⚙️ How REPACK Works

PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control, so an UPDATE creates a new row version and a DELETE leaves a dead tuple behind. Routine vacuuming makes that space reusable, but it doesn’t necessarily return space to the operating system or restore a useful physical row order. The usual fixes — VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER, or external tools such as pg_repack — take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the whole operation, blocking normal access to the table.

REPACK reclaims space like VACUUM FULL; with USING INDEX, it also physically orders rows like CLUSTER. With CONCURRENTLY, PostgreSQL rebuilds the table while normal reads and writes continue, capturing ongoing changes through logical decoding. It then takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock to apply any remaining captured changes and swap the new table and index files into place.

Component Role
pg_plan_advice Describes planner decisions as advice, applies supplied advice, reports whether it was followed
pg_stash_advice Stores advice by query ID and applies it automatically when a matching query is planned

These components do not add cross-table statistics or replace the planner. Instead, they let you intervene when an inaccurate estimate produces a poor plan. Unlike inline optimizer hints, plan advice lives outside the application’s query text. You can inspect the current plan, test focused advice, and then stash it by query ID.

⚠️ REPACK Limitations

Concurrent repacking creates an additional replication slot for the duration of the operation, so it needs free capacity under max_repack_replication_slots and a table with either a non-deferrable primary key or a suitable index-based replica identity. It also needs temporary disk space for a copy of the table and all its indexes, potentially plus a sort file up to the size of the table.

Tables with heavy update and delete traffic face an additional limit: the current upstream PostgreSQL 19 implementation fails if more than about 104 million tuples in the target table are updated or deleted while REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) is running. This counts changes made during the repack, not rows already in the table.

Concurrent repacking is also not MVCC-safe: after it commits, transactions using snapshots taken before the repack began can see the table as empty. Physical clustering also degrades as later writes arrive. REPACK CONCURRENTLY still needs planning, but it brings into core a job that previously required more downtime or an extension.

🚀 Availability

To try it, create a new Lakebase project and select PostgreSQL 19 as the version.

#PostgreSQL #Lakebase #Database #GARelease #REPACK #QueryPlanning

Source: PostgreSQL 19 is available on Lakebase

item.title: TypeSafe Jev Browser: Fast, Cheap, Headless Automation
item.description:
TypeSafe Jev Browser: Fast, Cheap, Headless Automation

TypeSafe released a new tool that lets developers drive a real headless browser with minimal cost and effort.

🔍 Overview

  • Provides fast and very cheap browser use via TypeSafe’s Jev model.
  • Accepts a task and a URL, and drives a real headless browser through an MCP server, CLI, or library.
  • Returns the final page, a step trace with confidences, console errors, and a screenshot.

🧩 How it Works

  • TypeSafe’s Jev model picks one action per step from the page’s clickable, typeable, and selectable elements, and scores how likely it is that the goal is met or the run is stuck.
  • Code owns the loop, managing budgets, recovery, and stop gates.

⚙️ Key Details

Env Variable Description
JEV_BROWSER_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD set to 1 to opt out of automatic Playwright Chromium download
JEV_BROWSER_AUTH_TOKEN required unless HOST is loopback
JEV_BROWSER_MAX_CONCURRENCY default 4; limits concurrent browsers
JEV_BROWSER_TRANSPORT set to http to use HTTP transport
HOST defaults to 127.0.0.1; set to 0.0.0.0 to serve beyond your machine
PORT default 8080
JEV_BROWSER_MAX_SECONDS default 180, capped at 600
  • Listens on PORT (default 8080) and serves MCP at /mcp, with a health check at /health.
  • --http and JEV_BROWSER_TRANSPORT=http are equivalent; containers and service units can select the transport without argv.
  • It speaks MCP 2026-07-28 and falls back to stateless serving for 2025‑era clients, keeping no sessions so any number of replicas can sit behind a plain load balancer.
  • Each in‑flight call runs its own headless Chromium for up to its time budget (max_seconds, default 180, cap 600). Admitted requests are capped at JEV_BROWSER_MAX_CONCURRENCY (default 4; excess gets 429).
  • Reverse proxy or load balancer read timeouts must be at least as long as the largest max_seconds you allow, or it will cut healthy runs short.
  • The server itself speaks plain HTTP; terminate TLS at a reverse proxy or load balancer before exposing it beyond loopback, and put connection limits and request rate limits at that ingress.

🚀 Availability

  • Requires Node.js 22 or newer.
  • Install from npm; Playwright’s Chromium downloads automatically on install unless JEV_BROWSER_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD=1.
  • The service listens on PORT (default 8080) and serves MCP at /mcp.
  • No session state; any number of replicas can sit behind a plain load balancer.

💡 Examples

  • Navigated Wikipedia from the Coffee article to Espresso in about 4 seconds, for $0.0016.
  • Pulled the price off a live pricing page.
  • Returned a full guide page as markdown.
  • Produced an accessibility‑tree breakdown of a WordPress site.
  • Filled a contact form and stopped without submitting it.

#JevBrowser #HeadlessAutomation #TypeSafe #NodeJS #WebAutomation

Source: jkudish/jev-browser

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and AgentCore Memory Integration
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and AgentCore Memory Integration

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory have been updated to include integrated conversation storage, fact extraction, and intelligent retrieval. This capability allows developers to streamline the process of maintaining context across sessions by automating fact-based retrieval and knowledge base interactions.

🧩 How it works

By adding a memoryConfiguration to the AgenticRetrieveStream request, AgentCore memory functions as a retrieval source alongside a knowledge base. The integration follows these operational steps:

  • Conversation Management: The service stores each conversation and extracts facts from it.
  • Planning: The planner autonomously decides when a stored fact about the user is relevant.
  • Query Composition: Retrieved facts are used to compose sub-queries sent to the knowledge base.
  • Persistence: After an answer is generated, the service saves the turn back to memory.

⚙️ Key details

The integration enables robust access control and user-specific memory, as illustrated by the following table of operational roles:

Component Role
Amazon Cognito Authenticates employees and provides sub and email claims
AgentCore Memory Stores facts, conversation history, and user context
Managed Knowledge Base Performs ACL-enabled retrieval based on user context
Planner Determines when to use long-term memory to aid sub-queries

💡 Implementation Requirements

  • Opt-in Compatibility: The feature is opt-in and backward compatible.
  • Security: The application remains responsible for authenticating the user and passing identity information. The userContext ensures the knowledge base returns only documents permitted by the user’s access control lists (ACLs).
  • IAM Roles: The handler assumes the application’s IAM role using the user ID as a session tag.

#AmazonBedrock #GenerativeAI #AIAgents #CloudComputing

Source: Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Browser Use releases Pi Mono-based web agent with cloud browser support
item.description:
Browser Use releases Pi Mono-based web agent with cloud browser support

Browser Use has announced a new AI web agent built on Pi Mono, described as a tiny TypeScript web agent that hill climbed on real browser evaluations. The agent writes JavaScript, controls Chrome, and builds the helpers it needs dynamically. It uses Pi Mono plus a persistent V8 REPL and raw CDP to enable programmability with sessions, saved logins, streaming and typed results. The implementation is provided as a single SDK that can be integrated into applications via npm install @browser_use/pi, pnpm add @browser_use/pi, or bun add @browser_use/pi. Developers need Node 22.19+ or Bun 1.3.14+ (with Bun requiring Node for the V8 worker). The system uses Browser Use Cloud, so no local Chrome installation is needed, and supports upstream Pi’s model catalog and transports with custom providers, sessions with follow-ups and saved logins, persistent workspaces, and cloud browsers or user-owned Chrome. An ultrafast mode minimizes waits after actions, and the platform provides interaction highlights, recordings, and GIF exports. JavaScript runs in a separate worker with filesystem and network access, while anonymous run counters are enabled by default but can be disabled through telemetry settings or the DO_NOT_TRACK environment variable.

#AIagents #TypeScript #webautomation #PiMono #BrowserAutomation

Source: browser-use/browser-use-pi

item.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a fast, efficient AI model for developers
item.description:
Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a fast, efficient AI model for developers

Today Google announced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a new model in the Gemini 4 family built for rapid, efficient execution of everyday coding and agentic workflows.

🔍 Overview

  • Hydrogen targets “rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows” while Carbon and Argon remain the frontier models for deep, long‑horizon reasoning.
  • It runs on a flat‑rate pricing of $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens across a 1 million‑token context window (both input and output).
  • Four thinking levels – low, medium, high (default), and xhigh – let users trade quality, latency, and cost predictably.
  • The model pairs native 1 M‑token input with up to 1 M‑token output to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and video into cited reports.

🧩 How it works

  • Hydrogen batches file‑read and search calls in parallel, enabling 2×‑2.8× faster repository exploration and 12%‑23% lower token usage compared with Gemini 3.8 Flash.
  • In multi‑step research or code‑base navigation it ranks #5 on Agent Arena and leads its class on HLE‑Diamond (58.8%), Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3% #1), Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8% tied #1), and AutomationBench‑AA.
  • On the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark it scores 53.4%, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 it scores 71.6%.
  • For developer‑centric tasks like live UI prototyping, design‑to‑code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional layouts with fewer prompts.

⚙️ Key details

Model Primary strength
Gemini 4 Carbon Deep, long‑horizon reasoning
Gemini 4 Argon Deep, long‑horizon reasoning
Gemini 4 Hydrogen Rapid, high‑throughput execution
  • Orchestrator (in Google Antigravity) automatically switches between models in a session. On Terminal‑Bench 4.0 it achieved near‑Carbon success rates while using 24% less quota and finishing 19% faster.
  • In multi‑agent workflows Carbon can coordinate while Hydrogen powers worker and verifier agents, allowing parallel development across isolated workspaces.
  • Compared with Gemini 3.8 Flash, Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5× faster at its high default setting, more than triples Terminal‑Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs 18.2%), and reduces fabricated claims by >5×.

🚀 Availability

  • Hydrogen is available to all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for Business, the Gemini app, Google Search, and to paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity.

💡 Why it matters

  • Teams can keep Carbon or Argon for deep architectural judgment while using Hydrogen as a disciplined execution engine for code writing, testing, and verification.
  • The lower latency and token‑efficient batching cut costs and speed up shipping of complex projects.
  • Improved instruction following, tone adherence, and tool‑calling make Hydrogen a reliable everyday assistant for drafting emails, study guides, and other documents.

#GoogleAI #Gemini #AIModels

Source: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base adds fine-grained access control and migration tools
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base adds fine-grained access control and migration tools

Amazon Bedrock now provides a Managed Knowledge Base service that handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval. This service includes built-in features such as hybrid search, a managed reranker, and multimodal file parsing, with infrastructure that scales automatically based on content volume.

🧩 How it works

Managed Knowledge Base simplifies content management by handling technical infrastructure, while allowing teams to retain control over their content and applications. The service integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to expose knowledge bases as tools for agents.

Feature Function
ACL awareness Filters retrieval results based on user permissions
Agentic retrieval Handles multi-part questions and iterative searching
Deletion safeguard Protects against accidental bulk removal of indexed content
Native connectors Ingests from S3, SharePoint, and Confluence

⚙️ Key details

  • Migration Support: A new migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps teams migrate from customer-managed knowledge bases to the managed service. The process includes read-only discovery, planning, and the generation of infrastructure-as-code templates.
  • Access Control: The system supports Access Control List (ACL) awareness, which ingests document permissions alongside content. When integrated with AgentCore Gateway, the system can inject verified user attributes into tool calls to ensure users only access authorized documents.
  • Security Layers: Security is maintained through a combination of request interceptors that define user context, Cedar policies within AgentCore, and resource-based policies that restrict access to the gateway execution role.
  • Pricing: The service uses usage-based pricing, with costs metered directly based on stored and retrieved content.

🚀 Availability

  • Supports up to 200 data sources per knowledge base.
  • Supports up to 10,000 knowledge bases per account, per Region.
  • Integration with AgentCore Gateway and resource-based policies are exclusive to Managed Knowledge Base.

#AmazonBedrock #GenerativeAI #CloudComputing #DataSecurity

Source: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent | Amazon Web Services Source: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Serverless Model Context Protocol Server Enables Shared Enterprise Data Access for AI Agents
item.description:
Serverless Model Context Protocol Server Enables Shared Enterprise Data Access for AI Agents

Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application.

🔍 Overview

  • “Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between.”
  • Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control.
  • As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi‑day engineering effort.
  • Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow.
  • To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate.

🧩 How it works

  1. Client layer – users submit a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53, reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet (HTTPS + AWS WAF), then routes to Amazon Cognito for authentication and enrichment. Authenticated traffic enters a private subnet where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate, stores session state in Amazon DynamoDB, and forwards requests through an internal ALB to the MCP server layer.
  2. MCP server layer – an AI agent powered by Amazon Bedrock orchestrates tools built with FastMCP (a Python framework for building MCP servers). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to every model interaction.
  3. Tools layer – Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift execute SQL against the data lake; Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (RAG) handles semantic search. AWS Lambda ingests data into Amazon S3 and the knowledge bases.
  4. Knowledge‑base refresh layer – a metadata catalog stores schema descriptions, column‑level semantics, and table relationships. It is refreshed continuously, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives.
  5. When a context specifies tables, the MCP server narrows its search of the metadata catalog to those tables, reducing noise and improving SQL generation accuracy.

⚙️ Key details

  • “Adding a dataset requires only a metadata file, not code.”
  • Access control is enforced at the MCP server layer, providing a single audit point.
  • The metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, allowing the agent to derive schema knowledge at query time – no hard‑coded table structures or redeployment when schemas change.
  • The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge‑base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable.
  • In testing, this scoping keeps end‑to‑end interaction latency in the 15–20 second range.
  • The data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain‑specific data.

🚀 Availability & Deployment

  • The MCP server is deployed serverlessly on Amazon ECS Fargate, eliminating the need for provisioned servers.
  • Public‑to‑private subnet routing ensures secure handling of authenticated traffic.
  • Amazon Route 53, Application Load Balancers, AWS WAF, Amazon Cognito, DynamoDB, Athena, Redshift, Bedrock Guardrails, and Lambda are all managed services that contribute to a fully managed solution.
  • FastMCP provides the framework for building MCP servers in Python, and Amazon Bedrock supplies the underlying LLM capabilities.

This implementation removes duplicated integration code, centralizes access control, and shortens onboarding of new datasets from multi‑day efforts to a simple metadata file drop.

#AIAgents #ModelContextProtocol #AWS #EnterpriseData

Source: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate | Amazon Web Services

item.title: OpenAI adds API credit benefit for $100‑$500 ChatGPT subscriptions
item.description:
OpenAI adds API credit benefit for $100‑$500 ChatGPT subscriptions

OpenAI announced that subscribers paying $100, $200, or $500 per month for ChatGPT now receive an equivalent amount of credits that can be applied to one of their API organizations. The move mirrors Anthropic’s benefit introduced earlier this month for Max and Team subscribers.

🔍 Overview

  • Anthropic introduced a benefit: $100, $200, and $500 per month subscribers receive the equivalent quantity of (expiring) credits for the Anthropic API.
  • OpenAI launched a very similar deal: $100, $200, or $500 subscription plans get the same quantity of credits to apply to an API organization.
  • The update was reported on 29 October 2026.

🧩 How it works

  • Eligible ChatGPT subscription tiers (the $100, $200, and $500 plans) automatically earn a matching number of API credits.
  • The credits are tied to an API organization owned by the subscriber.
  • Credits are expiring, matching the description used for Anthropic’s benefit.

⚙️ Key details

  • Subscription tiers: $100, $200, $500 per month.
  • Credit amount: Same numeric value as the subscription price (e.g., a $200 plan gets 200 credits).
  • Applicability: Credits can be used with the subscriber’s OpenAI API organization.
  • Reference: “API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions.”

🚀 Availability

  • The benefit is available to all current and new subscribers of the $100, $200, or $500 ChatGPT plans.
  • No additional actions are required; credits are automatically allocated.

💡 Why it matters

  • Users who maintain subscriptions with both Anthropic and OpenAI can leverage the same credit structure across both providers.
  • One user noted: “I maintain subscriptions with both companies, so this is great news for me!”
  • The same user added: “I may even ship some public‑facing demos now that the credits are already covered by my existing subscriptions.”

#OpenAI #Anthropic #APIcredits #ChatGPT #Subscriptions

Source: API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions

item.title: AWS Amazon Connect Customer Named Leader in 2026 Gartner CCaaS Magic Quadrant
item.description:
AWS Amazon Connect Customer Named Leader in 2026 Gartner CCaaS Magic Quadrant

item.title: Exowatt Deploys Edge AI Agents for Solar‑Powered Data Center Alarm Triage
item.description:
Exowatt Deploys Edge AI Agents for Solar‑Powered Data Center Alarm Triage

Exowatt has expanded its modular, dispatchable solar platform with AI agents that autonomously triage alarms and perform energy‑market analysis, using a serverless model‑customization pipeline on AWS.

🔍 Overview

  • Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems for energy‑intensive applications such as AI data centers.
  • The flagship Exowatt P3 captures solar energy with optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long‑duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand via a heat engine.
  • P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, avoiding multi‑year grid interconnection queues.
  • A fleet of AI agents monitors live alarms at the edge, where connectivity may be limited or absent.
  • The AI pipeline now turns raw operational data into a certified training set, a fine‑tuned model, and a deployed artifact in days rather than months.

🧩 How it works

Solar system

  • Optical lenses concentrate sunlight onto a thermal absorber.
  • Heat is stored in a thermal battery for long‑duration discharge.
  • A heat engine converts stored heat to electricity on demand.

AI pipeline

  • Raw alarm and market data are collected from each site.
  • Open‑weight base models are fine‑tuned with Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) on Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • Serverless training allocates capacity on demand, allowing multiple experiments per day.
  • The best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry and hosted via Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import.
  • Edge‑deployed models run on no‑GPU controllers; cloud‑deployed models run in the Cloud EMS.

AWS services powering the pipeline

Service Role
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import Hosts the fine‑tuned Qwen3‑14B for Cloud EMS (private invocation)
Amazon Bedrock (Qwen3‑VL‑235B) Provides paraphrasing for alarm‑triage
Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 4.6) Provides paraphrasing for energy‑market analysis
Amazon SageMaker AI (serverless model customization) Fine‑tunes open‑weight base models using LoRA and SFT
Amazon SageMaker AI Model Registry Stores and versions the evaluated deployment artifact

⚙️ Key details

  • Edge alarm‑triage uses the Qwen3‑1.7B model, fine‑tuned for the specific hardware and logic of Exowatt’s EMS.
  • Cloud energy‑market analysis uses the larger Qwen3‑14B model.
  • The fine‑tuned models achieve higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost.
  • Models are small enough to run on edge controllers without GPUs yet accurate enough for autonomous operation.
  • The pipeline can be reused to build smaller, task‑specific models across the growing fleet of sites.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables data centers to come online quickly without waiting for grid interconnection.
  • Provides reliable alarm monitoring even when connectivity is intermittent.
  • Reduces operational cost by avoiding per‑decision calls to large frontier models.
  • Accelerates model development from months to days, supporting rapid deployment as the fleet scales toward thousands of units.

#Exowatt #AIagents #SolarPower #AWS #EdgeAI

Source: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Atomic Agent Adds Snowflake Integration via Composio and MCP
item.description:
Atomic Agent Adds Snowflake Integration via Composio and MCP

Atomic Agent, the open‑source on‑device AI assistant, now supports direct interaction with Snowflake through the Composio integration and the Snowflake Model Context Protocol (MCP).

🔍 Overview

  • Atomic Agent runs on your machine and supports local models via llama.cpp.
  • Through Composio it can connect to 1,500+ apps, including Snowflake.
  • Users can issue natural‑language requests such as “list today’s new users” or “cancel a long‑running data import”; authentication is handled automatically.

🧩 How it works

  • Atomic Agent connects to Composio’s Tool Router over Streamable HTTP MCP.
  • For each request the agent discovers the appropriate tools; Composio supplies the necessary account authentication.
  • Execution and account‑connection tools obey the agent’s configured approval policy – you must review any approval prompt before the action proceeds.

⚙️ Setup & Usage

  • Requirements: Atomic Agent v0.5.6 or later, a Composio API key, and a Snowflake account.
  • Add the line below to ~/.atomic‑agent/.env, replacing the placeholder with your key, then start Atomic Agent: 
    1

    COMPOSIO_API_KEY=YOUR_COMPOSIO_API_KEY
  • In Atomic Agent, open the Integrations tab, select Composio, press e, paste the API key, and press Enter. The tools become available immediately, without a restart.
  • Ask Atomic Agent to perform an action in Snowflake. The agent searches Composio for the correct tool. On first use, a sign‑in link is returned in the chat – follow it to connect your Snowflake account, then return to Atomic Agent to continue.

🚀 Availability

  • The Hobby plan includes 100,000 tool calls per month.
  • Integration can be disabled by setting "composio": { "enabled": false } in the config; the saved key remains on disk.

📋 Tool Reference

Tool What it does
Cancel Statement Execution Cancels the execution of a running SQL statement

The Snowflake MCP server implements the Model Context Protocol, giving the agent structured and secure access to the data warehouse and service status. It enables the agent to execute SQL, explore databases and tables, track or cancel statements, inspect catalog integrations, and monitor incidents and maintenance on your behalf.

#AtomicAgent #Snowflake #Composio #AIAgents #MCP

item.title: Amazon Quick adds real‑time ACL checks to Bedrock Knowledge Bases for secure RAG
item.description:
Amazon Quick adds real‑time ACL checks to Bedrock Knowledge Bases for secure RAG

Enterprise organizations are adopting Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to unlock insights from company knowledge sources like Microsoft SharePoint, Google Drive, and Atlassian Confluence. Because those sources contain sensitive information governed by complex permission structures, making sure AI‑generated answers respect those permissions is one of the hardest challenges in enterprise AI.

🔍 Overview

  • RAG solutions must enforce access controls that match the source systems.
  • A single unauthorized document in an AI response could expose confidential strategy, unreleased financial data, or sensitive HR information.
  • Organizations want to democratize AI‑powered insights without compromising their existing security posture.

⚠️ Weaknesses of snapshot‑based ACLs

  • Data source connectors (e.g., SharePoint connector) pull ACLs during periodic sync jobs.
  • ACLs are stored as attributes in an index and used for pre‑retrieval filtering.
  • This model places sole enforcement responsibility on the AI system, which is not the authoritative source of permissions.
  • Pull‑based syncs create a snapshot; the ACLs reflect the state at the last sync.
  • Sources like Confluence do not emit events when group membership changes, so revoked access may still be honored until the next sync.
  • New permission features or changes to sharing models can create gaps in the ACL mapping logic.

✅ Real‑time ACL enforcement in Amazon Quick & Bedrock Knowledge Bases

When a user queries an Amazon Quick agent backed by a Google Drive knowledge base, the system enforces access controls in two stages:

  1. Pre‑retrieval filtering – Amazon Quick performs a semantic search against the vector index, then applies the stored ACL attributes. This reduces the number of documents that need real‑time checks.
  2. Real‑time verification – For the candidate documents, Amazon Quick calls the Google Drive APIs using a service‑account credential supplied by the administrator. It generates user‑specific access tokens through impersonation, and Google Drive, the source of truth for ACLs, confirms whether the user can view each document. Unauthorized documents are excluded before the passages are passed to the large language model (LLM).
Stage Action
Pre‑retrieval Semantic search + apply stored ACL attributes (index‑based filter)
Real‑time verification Call source API (Google Drive) with impersonated token; exclude documents without access

Additional safeguards such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, grounding checks, and configurable safety policies are applied to the LLM context.

💡 Why it matters

  • Always‑current permissions – No security gaps between sync cycles; revoking a user’s access is reflected in AI responses within moments, not hours or days.
  • Compliance assurance – The authoritative source (Google Drive, SharePoint, etc.) validates every document at query time.
  • Scalable cost – The two‑stage approach avoids costly real‑time API calls for every indexed passage while still guaranteeing up‑to‑date enforcement.

The combined solution lets enterprises democratize AI insights while maintaining strict security and compliance controls.

#RAG #AmazonBedrock #AIsecurity #EnterpriseAI

Source: Rethinking access control for RAG with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Confidence‑Gated Hybrid Beats Pure Models for Emotion Recognition in Call Centers
item.description:
Confidence‑Gated Hybrid Beats Pure Models for Emotion Recognition in Call Centers

Emotion recognition in conversation (ERC) is a production capability behind agent‑assist prompts, escalation routing, and post‑call analytics in contact‑center‑as‑a‑service (CCaaS) platforms, where cost and latency constraints matter as much as accuracy.

🔍 Overview

  • Three deployment options were compared: a low‑cost stacked ensemble, off‑the‑shelf LLM prompting (GPT‑4o‑mini), and a confidence‑gated hybrid that escalates only the ensemble’s least‑confident predictions to the LLM.
  • The hybrid mirrors IVA‑to‑human‑agent escalation policies used in production contact centers.

🧩 How it works

  • Ensemble: stacked model using sentence embeddings, windowed context, and RandomForest/XGBoost/logistic‑regression stacking.
  • LLM: GPT‑4o‑mini prompted zero‑shot, few‑shot, or chain‑of‑thought.
  • Hybrid: the ensemble handles the majority of utterances; when its confidence falls below a threshold, the turn is routed to the LLM for re‑prediction.
  • Escalated turns disproportionately follow an emotion or sentiment shift, providing an interpretable routing signal. The ensemble’s confidence is well‑calibrated and tends to be under‑confident rather than over‑confident.

⚙️ Performance comparison

Option Approach Cost per M utterances Latency Weighted F1 (IEMOCAP)
Ensemble Stacked ensemble (sentence embeddings, windowed context, RandomForest/XGBoost/logistic‑regression stacking) near‑zero <10 ms 0.595
LLM GPT‑4o‑mini prompting (zero‑shot, few‑shot, chain‑of‑thought) $99‑170 – 0.460‑0.536
Hybrid Confidence‑gated cascade (ensemble + LLM escalation) $10‑85 – 0.620 (IEMOCAP) 0.643 (MELD) 0.824 (CMU‑MOSI)
  • On IEMOCAP the ensemble outperforms every LLM configuration (0.595 vs. 0.460‑0.536, p < 0.0001).
  • On MELD and CMU‑MOSI the ranking reverses, so neither pure system is a safe default.
  • The hybrid Pareto‑dominates both pure systems on all three datasets, routing most traffic through the near‑zero‑cost ensemble.

💡 Why it matters

  • The hybrid reduces spend from roughly $99‑170 per million utterances (LLM‑only) to $10‑85 while delivering higher accuracy.
  • It provides an auditable escalation signal tied to emotion shifts, aligning with operational needs in CCaaS.
  • Confidence‑gated cascading, a known technique in ML, is shown to transfer cleanly to dialogue‑contextual ERC, offering a concrete deployment recipe for conversational‑AI platforms.

#EmotionRecognition #ContactCenterAI #LLMDeployment

Source: When to Call an LLM: A Confidence-Gated Hybrid for Cost-Effective Emotion Recognition in Conversational AI

item.title: Serverless Framework V4 Adds AI Agent Support and AWS Enhancements
item.description:
Serverless Framework V4 Adds AI Agent Support and AWS Enhancements

The Serverless Framework has released version 4, introducing significant updates that enhance serverless application development on AWS. This release emphasizes AI integration, security, and developer experience improvements.

🔍 Overview

The Serverless Framework is a command-line tool enabling developers to deploy serverless applications using approachable YAML syntax. It supports AWS Lambda and other managed services, offering auto-scaling, zero idle costs, and minimal maintenance. Version 4 expands these capabilities with AI-native features and AWS ecosystem integrations.

🚀 Key New Features

  • Sandboxes: Isolate ephemeral compute environments on AWS Lambda for untrusted workloads like AI agents or per-session code execution.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Support: Define AI agents, memory, tools, and code interpreters directly in serverless.yml using the ai property.
  • AWS Login & SSO: Streamline AWS credential setup via browser-based flows.
  • Deployment Diffs: Preview CloudFormation stack changes before deployment using serverless diff.
  • Managed Instances: Native EC2-backed Lambda support for higher throughput and long-running workloads.
  • Durable Functions: Built-in stateful workflows for complex orchestrations.
  • Lambda Tenant Isolation: Reduce cross-tenant interference in multi-tenant applications.
  • HTTP Response Streaming: Stream long-running AI responses from Lambda via API Gateway.
  • Serverless MCP: IDE integration to debug serverless apps directly in editors like Cursor or Windsurf.

🛠️ Enhanced Developer Experience

Popular plugins are now built-in, including Python requirements and API Gateway Service Proxy. Custom domains with auto-configured SSL are now natively supported. Secrets management integrates with Doppler via framework variables.

💡 Why It Matters

These updates position the Serverless Framework as a robust platform for AI-driven and enterprise-scale serverless applications. Features like Sandboxes and AgentCore support accelerate secure AI agent deployment, while MCP integration eliminates context-switching during debugging. The framework now unifies deployment across AWS SAM, CloudFormation, and traditional Serverless projects.

⚙️ Under the Hood

Version 4 maintains multi-language support (Node.js, Python, Go, etc.) and extensibility via 1,000+ plugins. All features are actively maintained by Serverless Inc., ensuring long-term reliability.

#Serverless #AWS #AIAgents #DevOps #CloudNative

Source: serverless/serverless

item.title: OpenCode Go Offers $10/month Access to Reliable Open Coding Models
item.description:
OpenCode Go Offers $10/month Access to Reliable Open Coding Models

OpenCode has launched OpenCode Go, a $10‑per‑month subscription that provides reliable, low‑latency access to popular open‑source coding models.

🔍 Overview

  • Open models now perform close to proprietary models on coding tasks.
  • Reliable, low‑latency access to these models can be difficult because provider quality and availability vary.
  • OpenCode Go addresses this gap with a stable global service, especially for international users.

🧩 How it works

  • Subscribe to OpenCode Go and receive an API key.
  • The service functions like any other provider in the OpenCode platform.
  • It is optional; users can still use OpenCode without the subscription.
  • Designed for OpenCode and similar coding agents that send comparable request types.
  • Traffic is monitored to prevent abuse that could degrade other users’ experience.

⚙️ Key details

  • Pricing: $10 per month.
  • Usage limits are expressed as monthly dollar amounts; each model enforces:
    • 5‑hour limit: 20 % of the monthly limit
    • Weekly limit: 50 % of the monthly limit
    • Monthly limit: 100 % of the monthly limit
  • Token pricing is listed per 1 M tokens (exact amounts are model‑specific).
  • The list of available models may change as new models are tested and added.
  • The x‑opencode‑session header request remains open, but sending that header is no longer required.
  • Clients beyond OpenCode have been validated, though future support is not guaranteed and some have incomplete session support.

🚀 Availability

  • Subscription costs $10/month and provides stable global access.
  • Primarily aimed at international users seeking consistent performance.
  • Works with the latest version v0.81.6 or later, which includes the session‑header fix.

💡 Why it matters

  • Open models have improved to near‑proprietary performance, offering a cheaper alternative for coding tasks.
  • Because many providers can serve these models competitively, costs are generally lower than closed‑source options.
  • OpenCode Go bundles reliable, low‑latency access into a simple subscription, reducing the overhead of managing multiple providers.

#OpenCode #OpenSourceAI #CodingModels

Source: Go
